key_terms.meaning: Frequency where gain is 0.707 of midband; set by coupling and bypass capacitors.
Flat-region gain between f<sub>L</sub> and f<sub>H</sub>.
Series capacitor between stages; its reactance rises at low frequency and reduces gain.
Capacitor across an emitter or source resistor; removes ac degeneration only above a low frequency.
Base-emitter capacitance in the hybrid-pi BJT model; part of input capacitance.
Collector-base capacitance in the hybrid-pi model; causes Miller effect.
Input capacitance appears as C<sub>μ</sub>(1+|A<sub>v</sub>|), lowering f<sub>H</sub>.
Frequency where gain falls to 0.707 of midband because of internal capacitances.
For a dominant-pole amplifier, midband gain × bandwidth is constant.
Frequency where open-loop current or voltage gain magnitude falls to 1.
CE input stage followed by CB stage; reduces Miller effect and extends bandwidth.
Load is a resonant LC circuit; high gain near f<sub>0</sub> and narrow bandwidth.
Part of the input cycle, in degrees, during which the transistor conducts.
dc operating point with no signal; sets class, efficiency and distortion.
Bias between class A and B; removes crossover dead zone with small quiescent current.
Two devices drive opposite half-cycles into the load.
Dead-zone distortion near zero crossing in class B due to V<sub>BE</sub> turn-on.
Pulse-width modulation; duty cycle represents the signal in a class D switch.
Total harmonic distortion; rms harmonic voltage divided by fundamental, often in percent.
Metal thermal path that lowers θ<sub>JA</sub> and keeps T<sub>J</sub> below T<sub>J(max)</sub>.

takeaways: Coupling and bypass capacitors set the lower cut-off frequency; above f<sub>L</sub> they act nearly as short circuits.
Internal C<sub>π</sub> and C<sub>μ</sub> set the upper cut-off frequency; the Miller effect multiplies C<sub>μ</sub> at the input.
A dominant-pole amplifier has a constant gain-bandwidth product, and f<sub>T</sub> is its unity-gain frequency.
Wideband design trades gain for bandwidth using cascode or CC-CE stages, while tuned design trades bandwidth for gain at f<sub>0</sub>.
Power amplifier classes are distinguished by conduction angle, and efficiency rises as conduction angle falls.
A push-pull class B stage uses two devices for opposite half-cycles, and class AB bias removes crossover distortion.
Class C uses short conduction and a tuned load for RF, while class D switches with PWM for high efficiency.
THD measures unwanted harmonics, and a heat sink controls junction temperature and device reliability.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine a sketched frequency-response or class waveform with a derivation and an efficiency, THD or thermal calculation.

bank.q: Define lower and upper cut-off frequencies. Explain why an RC-coupled amplifier has a flat midband between them.
outline: State f<sub>L</sub> and f<sub>H</sub> as 0.707 of midband gain.
Explain coupling and bypass capacitors at low frequency.
Explain internal capacitances and Miller effect at high frequency.
Sketch the Bode magnitude plot and mark bandwidth = f<sub>H</sub> − f<sub>L</sub>.

bank.q: Explain the Miller effect in a common-emitter amplifier using the hybrid-pi model.
outline: Draw C<sub>μ</sub> between base and collector.
Show input capacitance C<sub>in</sub> ≈ C<sub>π</sub> + C<sub>μ</sub>(1+|A<sub>v</sub>|).
Explain why this lowers f<sub>H</sub>.
State that cascode reduces Miller multiplication.

bank.q: Define gain-bandwidth product and transition frequency. Derive their relation for a dominant-pole amplifier.
outline: Write |A(f)| = A<sub>0</sub>/√(1+(f/f<sub>p</sub>)²).
State GBW = A<sub>0</sub>f<sub>p</sub>.
At f<sub>T</sub>, |A(f<sub>T</sub>)| = 1.
For a dominant pole, f<sub>T</sub> ≈ GBW.

bank.q: Classify power amplifiers by conduction angle and quiescent point. State one use of each class.
outline: Class A: 360°, high quiescent current, low distortion.
Class B: 180°, zero quiescent current, crossover distortion.
Class AB: 180° to 360°, small bias, audio use.
Class C: less than 180°, tuned RF use; class D: switching, PWM.

bank.q: A dominant-pole amplifier has midband gain 1000 and upper cut-off frequency 10 kHz. Find GBW, f<sub>T</sub> and gain at 100 kHz.
outline: GBW = 1000 × 10 kHz = 10 MHz.
For a dominant pole, f<sub>T</sub> ≈ 10 MHz.
At 100 kHz, gain ≈ GBW/f = 10<sup>7</sup>/10<sup>5</sup> = 100.
State the dominant-pole assumption.

bank.q: A dual-supply class B push-pull stage uses ±15 V and an 8 Ω load. At maximum sine output, calculate output power, supply power, efficiency and per-device dissipation.
outline: V<sub>p</sub> = 15 V.
P<sub>out(max)</sub> = V<sub>p</sub>²/(2R<sub>L</sub>) = 15²/(2×8) = 14.1 W.
P<sub>dc</sub> = (2/π)(V<sub>CC</sub>²/R<sub>L</sub>) = 17.9 W.
η = P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>dc</sub> = π/4 = 78.5%.
Total dissipation = 3.8 W; per device ≈ 1.9 W at this point.

bank.q: Explain how a cascode amplifier and a CC-CE cascade extend bandwidth. State the gain-bandwidth trade-off.
outline: Cascode: CE input feeds CB stage; collector-base swing of input device is small.
Small Miller multiplication gives lower input capacitance and higher f<sub>H</sub>.
CC-CE: emitter follower buffers source resistance before the CE gain stage.
Both trade voltage gain or output swing for wider bandwidth.

bank.q: A tuned amplifier is centred at 1 MHz with Q = 50. Calculate its bandwidth and half-power frequencies. State the effect of doubling Q.
outline: BW = f<sub>0</sub>/Q = 1 MHz/50 = 20 kHz.
Half-power frequencies are 990 kHz and 1010 kHz.
Doubling Q halves bandwidth to 10 kHz.
Higher Q gives higher selectivity and narrower band.

bank.q: Explain class AB push-pull biasing and show how it removes crossover distortion.
outline: Class B has a dead zone while V<sub>BE</sub> < 0.7 V.
Class AB uses diodes or V<sub>BE</sub> multiplier bias.
Small quiescent current keeps one device on near zero crossing.
Sketch combined transfer characteristic with no flat dead zone.
Efficiency is slightly below class B.

bank.q: Compare class A, B, AB, C and D power amplifiers for conduction angle, efficiency, distortion and application. Choose a class for battery audio and for RF transmission.
outline: Give a table of conduction angle, Q point and maximum efficiency.
Class A: low distortion, low efficiency, 360°.
Class B/AB: push-pull audio; AB removes crossover distortion.
Class C: tuned RF, high efficiency, high distortion.
Class D: PWM switching, very high efficiency.
Justify class AB or D for battery audio and class C for RF.

bank.q: A transistor has T<sub>J(max)</sub> = 150°C, θ<sub>JC</sub> = 2°C/W, θ<sub>CS</sub> = 1°C/W, θ<sub>SA</sub> = 4°C/W and ambient 40°C. Find the maximum dissipation with the heat sink. Evaluate the case without a heat sink if θ<sub>JA</sub> = 60°C/W.
outline: Use T<sub>J</sub> = T<sub>A</sub> + P<sub>D</sub>(θ<sub>JC</sub> + θ<sub>CS</sub> + θ<sub>SA</sub>).
With heat sink θ<sub>JA</sub> = 7°C/W.
Without heat sink P<sub>D(max)</sub> = 110/60 = 1.83 W.
Conclude the heat sink raises safe dissipation about eight times.

bank.q: An amplifier has midband gain 200, f<sub>L</sub> = 50 Hz and f<sub>H</sub> = 200 kHz. Find bandwidth, GBW and gain at 2 MHz for a dominant high-frequency pole. Evaluate its use for audio from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
outline: BW ≈ 200 kHz − 50 Hz ≈ 199.95 kHz.
GBW ≈ 200 × 200 kHz = 40 MHz.
At 2 MHz, gain ≈ 40 MHz/2 MHz = 20.
At 20 Hz, gain is below 0.707 of midband because 20 Hz < f<sub>L</sub>.
It is flat over most of the audio band but not at the low end.

bank.q: Explain harmonic distortion and THD. Discuss how clipping, crossover distortion and temperature affect measured THD and reliability, and state the role of a heat sink.
outline: Define harmonics as 2f, 3f, ... components.
THD = √(V<sub>2</sub>² + V<sub>3</sub>² + ...)/V<sub>1</sub> × 100%.
Clipping adds odd harmonics.
Crossover distortion adds high-order harmonics near zero crossing.
Temperature shifts Q point and increases leakage; heat sink lowers θ<sub>JA</sub>.
Lower junction temperature improves reliability.

glossary.def: A plot or description of gain and phase against signal frequency.
Frequency where gain magnitude is 0.707 times its midband value.
Logarithmic ratio defined as 20 log<sub>10</sub>(V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>) for voltage.
Straight-line approximation of magnitude or phase response against log frequency.
Small-signal BJT model using resistances and capacitances such as r<sub>π</sub>, C<sub>π</sub> and C<sub>μ</sub>.
Effective input capacitance caused by a feedback capacitor between input and output.
Pole that is much lower in frequency than other poles and sets the bandwidth.
Difference between upper and lower cut-off frequencies, f<sub>H</sub> − f<sub>L</sub>.
Amplifier designed for large bandwidth, usually by giving up gain or reducing Miller effect.
Two BJTs connected so current gain is approximately the product of their β values.
Ratio f<sub>0</sub>/BW for a tuned circuit; higher Q means narrower bandwidth.
Ratio of useful output power to dc supply power, often expressed in percent.
Power amplifier class in which the device conducts for the full 360° cycle.
Power amplifier class in which each device conducts for about 180° of the cycle.
Power amplifier class with conduction angle below 180°, used with a tuned load.
Switching power amplifier class using pulse-width modulation and devices driven on or off.
Class A stage with the load connected directly in series with the transistor output path.
Amplifier whose load is connected through a transformer, allowing impedance matching and larger swing.
Temperature rise per watt of dissipation, measured in °C/W.
Temperature of the transistor silicon junction during operation.
Distortion caused when the output reaches a supply rail or saturation limit and is flattened.
Component at an integer multiple of the signal frequency, such as 2f or 3f.
Line on the output characteristic showing possible collector current and voltage for a given load.
Region of voltage, current and power in which a transistor can operate without damage.
